claims.claim_text: The Arduino board carries no distinguishing hardware: a socketed microcontroller, a shield expansion header and almost no support circuitry. What differentiates the platform is the software layer wrapped around that part, originally the Wiring programming interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't really have any support, um, circuitry around. It's got the expansion header, of course, the shield, um, header
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bringing analogue inputs out on the board itself removes an early obstacle: without on-board analogue-to-digital conversion a designer must add and talk to a separate converter before reading any sensor.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've already got analog built into it. And so that right there is pretty, pretty great for interfacing to a lot of devices
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The Arduino hardware is released under a licence that permits a third party to manufacture a board with identical layout and pinouts; nothing in the design files restrains reproduction.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no license that says you can't manufacture your own
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: The project separates the open hardware licence from the name: the design files may be copied and an identical board produced, but Arduino is a trademark and cannot be applied to the result.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you can take the exact same files, produce the exact same board, but you're not allowed to call it the Arduino.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: No open-source licence restrains offshore reproduction of a board; the choice of licence changes nothing about whether a design will be copied and sold at a lower price.
claims.quote_verbatim: But then you can't stop China. It doesn't matter which license you use.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: An open hardware design gives its originator no protection against a competitor manufacturing the same board at volume and undercutting them; this is the structural weakness of an open hardware business.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could come along and make an Arduino board tomorrow, get it manufactured in China and undercut the Arduino team and put them out of business probably.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A full Arduino board carries USB interface, regulator and connector circuitry that an embedded application does not use, so embedding a thirty to forty dollar board is expensive relative to the function drawn on; the cut-down variants exist to strip that overhead.
claims.quote_verbatim: to put a full Arduino board in there which costs $30 or $40 is expensive
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: Reusable module designs should hold to 0.1-inch pin spacing, the grid the Arduino header uses, so that others can breadboard and stack against them.
claims.quote_verbatim: use standard pin spacing. So, I mean, that is one of the things about the Arduino is, you know, 100-mil spacing.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: A modular system defined at schematic level survives reuse better than one defined at board level, because a fixed board imposes a form factor, a part choice, a supply voltage and a power budget that will not suit the next design.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if you start talking, oh, like a modular PCB level system, that's where it starts to break down and not work very well because it doesn't, oh, it doesn't suit somebody's form factor or it uses a part that you can't get now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: The classic Arduino's analogue input spans zero to five volts against the internal reference rather than a precision external voltage reference, which limits absolute measurement accuracy.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it uses the internal voltage reference. It doesn't use like a proper precision external reference
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: Some microcontroller crystal oscillator circuits need a resistor in parallel with the crystal to bias the inverter into its linear region; the AVR does not, and a board that shipped with that resistor absent still ran correctly.
claims.quote_verbatim: apparently some crystal oscillator circuits on microcontrollers need to have a bias resistor in order for the oscillator to function. And it seems like the AVR does not
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A component that is not electrically necessary may still be fitted for radiated-emissions margin during certification, and a functional power-on test will not detect its absence, which is how a board missing a part passes electrical test and ships.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's possible that they added the resistor there to improve like high frequency noise or some kind of like an EMI or RFI issue, because I know that these boards were FCC tested
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Missing-component escapes on an assembly line are caught with automated optical inspection that checks every board for absent or misplaced parts as it leaves the line, rather than relying on a functional test.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino team is investing in a visual inspection system, like an automated visual inspection system so that as boards come through their manufacturing line
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The platform is positioned as a springboard for physical computing work such as stage props and product prototypes, reaching working embedded behaviour without committing to a custom printed circuit board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to invest in actually making a custom printed circuit board or a custom embedded system, you can use the Arduino kind of as a springboard
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Bare AVR or PIC development requires configuring registers by hand before any peripheral does anything, so that opening a serial port or toggling one bit costs real effort; the Arduino libraries exist to remove that step.
claims.quote_verbatim: how much work goes into just setting up and getting a program running on a pick or an AVR, you know, it's quite a lot of work

claims.claim_text: Sustained open hardware platforms are produced by resourced companies rather than individuals: around 2011 the Arduino organisation turned over roughly five million dollars a year, Adafruit about a million and SparkFun about ten million.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're a $5 million a year company or something. You know, they're getting very large.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The overwhelming majority of users of an open hardware product buy the finished, supported board rather than building from the published files, so an open design with nobody manufacturing and supporting it at a good price does not reach users at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd go as far to say as 99% of Arduinos are used by people who just buy the finished product and hook stuff up to it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: chipKIT, built by Digilent around Microchip's PIC32, put a 32-bit part behind the Arduino programming model in two boards, the Uno32 and the Max32, matching the Uno and Mega outlines.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is now a Microchip Pick compatible 32-bit version of the Arduino. It's called the Chip Kit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: Prototyping on an Arduino commits the eventual product to the ATmega, because the code and libraries are written against that part; a compatible platform on a different architecture reopens the choice of production microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm locked into the Atmega chip because I designed the prototype with Arduino
claims.speaker: Jeremy Blum
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: The value of a standardised development board is that published example circuits and code apply unchanged to every user's board, the same property that made the Commodore 64 and Apple II useful to develop for.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's because everyone's running the same hardware. And so that means that the examples for any one circuit
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: A defining property of the Arduino is that it needs no external programmer: the board attaches directly to USB, whereas an equivalent PIC development board carries a second chip acting as in-circuit debugger and programmer.
claims.quote_verbatim: The whole idea of the Arduino is that you don't need an external programmer. It plugs straight up to the USB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: Programmer-free loading is achieved with resident bootloader firmware inside the microcontroller that accepts a new sketch over the serial link; a PIC-based equivalent instead needs a second chip to provide that interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: It needs an external Pic. It needs a second chip to act as an interface
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: The Parallax Basic Stamp anticipated the same mechanism a decade earlier: it shipped with a bootloader already programmed into the part, so a program could be dumped in over a serial port with no dedicated programmer.
claims.quote_verbatim: It, it had the bootloader in there actually pre-programmed in and you can hook it up to a serial port.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The irregular gap between two blocks of the Arduino header began as a layout mistake that was then carried forward for compatibility, so every shield since has had to reproduce it.
claims.quote_verbatim: So that's the case with the pin spacing is somebody made a mistake and now the shields all have that weird pin spacing on them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: The Arduino Leonardo moved the USB interface into the main microcontroller by using an ATmega32U4, removing the separate USB-to-serial chip; PJRC's Teensy had already used the same approach.
claims.quote_verbatim: an Arduino based around an Atmega 32U4 microcontroller that includes the USB functionality in the same microcontroller as what's running the Arduino code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: The Arduino Due broke the 8-bit AVR line by running an Atmel SAM3X ARM Cortex-M3 at 96 MHz.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino Due, I guess, which is an Arduino that runs on an ARM Cortex M3 running at 96 megahertz
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: The ArduPilot autopilot ran a working multirotor control loop on an 8-bit processor at roughly sixty to seventy per cent of its capacity, which places autopilot quality in the control algorithms rather than in clock speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a really good performing autopilot out there on basically an 8-bit processor
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The InvenSense MPU-6000 contains a digital motion processor that performs sensor fusion inside the chip, freeing that work from the flight controller.
claims.quote_verbatim: has a built-in processor right in the chip, which does sensor fusion. It's called digital motion processor
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Extra processing headroom on a flight controller is spent on running the estimation loop faster, for instance sensor fusion at 400 Hz instead of 100 or 200 Hz, and on hosting a real-time operating system so that adding a feature cannot disturb the timing of existing ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than doing our sensor fusion at 100 hertz or 200 hertz, maybe do it at 400 hertz
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Open source hardware is distributed under a licence rather than placed in the public domain, so a company cannot simply take the design, close it and sell it as its own.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a legal license behind the Arduino and most open source hardware stuff.
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: The Arduino Ethernet puts Ethernet on an Uno-class board but omits the USB interface, so programming it needs an external FTDI cable.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is a board called the Arduino Ethernet, which is based on the Uno with Ethernet on board, but it doesn't have a USB interface, which means that you need an FTDI cable or something similar to program it.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Once a network stack, some data storage and general input and output are added, a 328-class part runs out of pins and memory, which is the argument for pairing Ethernet with the larger Mega-class microcontroller instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: by the time you add the software stack necessary to do your network connectivity and you want to store a bit of data and do some IO, you quickly run out of pins and memory and things on a standard AT-Mega 328 type platform
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: A vehicle can be put permanently online with a low-power router-based computer and 3G modem in the boot, a microcontroller wired into the ignition system for start, stop and locking, and an OBD-II link into the engine management system for live data and position logging.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I actually got an Arduino and wired it into the ignition system of the car and connected that back to the computer.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Because the platform hides register configuration, clocking and input-output setup, coursework whose purpose is to teach those mechanisms excludes it.
claims.quote_verbatim: At this level of education, they're supposed to be learning the stuff that Arduino hides from you.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: Running a Wi-Fi stack on the same 8-bit microcontroller that runs the sketch consumes most of the available resources, which is why plug-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules normally carry their own processor for the stack and expose a simple SPI or I2C interface to the host.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a reason why those Wi-Fi modules have their own dedicated processing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: The Arduino execution model is a single sequential program running in a loop; adding networking usually forces a real-time operating system, and a full Linux stack on the same board is no longer deterministic.
claims.quote_verbatim: Easy to write a sequential program that just runs in a loop. But when you start doing Wi-Fi type stuff or networking type stuff, sometimes you need to get into, like, real-time operating systems
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: The Arduino download bundles a specific build of avrdude and the rest of the toolchain, so the user gets a known-good baseline instead of installing and version-matching the flashing utility separately.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not like you've got to go and install AVR, dude, separately. It's already handled, you know, and baselined for you.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: Duplicate implementations proliferate in the library ecosystem, with a search for an Arduino infrared library returning pages of independent versions; experienced engineers still rewrite them after being burned by days spent debugging someone else's code.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like 20 pages of everyone's written their own ir library
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyperloop, Upverter and Soldering - Unbelievable USB Ustulater

claims.claim_text: PC/104 established the stacking-board pattern long before the Arduino: a standardised outline with defined mounting holes and 0.1-inch board-to-board header pins functionally equivalent to the PC ISA bus, in 8- and 16-bit versions, with male pins below and female above so boards stack indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they're 0.1 inch header pins and they're in the, and they're functionally equivalent to the old PC ISA bus.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The PC/104 board measures about 90 by 96 millimetres and takes its number from the 104 pins of its bus connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's a standardized size. It's 90 by 96 millimeters.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: What makes a board an Arduino is the development environment rather than the header layout: the code must compile and run under the Arduino IDE against its libraries, and everything else is optional.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got to execute without fail under the arduino ide that's it and that's all it comes down to is the ide everything else is optional
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: The Arduino headers are a prototyping and stacking convenience; a custom board normally drops them and routes the signals where the design needs them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing anything custom you generally won't be using the arduino headers because it's it's just for prototyping and stacking
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: Technically the platform is ordinary C with a set of pre-written libraries plus an editor that compiles and downloads to the board in one step; the novelty is packaging rather than language.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still c you know it's still basic c it just has you know a lot of pre-compiled uh libraries
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: The ATmega beneath the abstraction is a production-worthy part, so a project that outgrows the environment's memory or timing limits can keep the same silicon and add a JTAG debugger rather than change architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: underneath the Arduino-ness, there's a beautiful processor. I mean, that Etmega is just a really cute little processor that I would use in products.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Using the platform still requires embedded programming and electronics knowledge, and anything web-connected adds networking and web services on top; those are the barriers a consumer-level product has to remove.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino always had the impediments of needing to know, you know, a little bit of embedded programming, electronics. And if you wanted to connect anything to the web, you need to know networking and web services as well.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: The MaKey MaKey is an Arduino with capacitive input pads that enumerates as a USB human interface device and issues key presses when a pad is touched, while remaining reprogrammable as an ordinary Arduino; SparkFun manufactured and shipped 11,000 units of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: made this product and shipped 11,000 units
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Arduino at Heart is a licensing programme that lets a third-party product carry an Arduino mark on the basis that Arduino technology sits at its core, as an alternative to the product being taken into the official board line.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino at heart is a program by Arduino for products that have Arduino technologies at their core.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A genuine Arduino sold for roughly twenty to thirty dollars while clone boards of essentially identical function were available for eight to ten dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can also buy a clone Arduino for $8, $10 on eBay
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We're Sorry! But Apple Ain't! - Remorseless RAM Racketeering

claims.claim_text: A reseller of Arduinos or clones has no room to charge a premium, because the product is identical everywhere and the price is therefore set at the bottom of the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're selling Arduinos or Arduino clones, for example, you've set up an online store, then you've got to sell them at a rock bottom price. Otherwise, you can't compete
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: A stackable form factor lets the expensive or scarce board be reused: the controller lifts off a wired-up stack of shields and moves to another project while the shields stay connected.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can take the Arduino off and leave your shields all hooked up to, uh, whatever it was you had and, and move that, that card around.
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: Energia is a fork of the Arduino project that compiles Wiring sketches for TI Launchpad boards; because the upstream IDE carried mostly Arduino targets, forking was the route to supporting other silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've forked their project on GitHub and created our own open source project called Energia
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: The Light Blue Bean is an Arduino-compatible Bluetooth Low Energy board with no connectors at all: it is programmed wirelessly over BLE rather than through any wired port.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has no connectors. So there's no way – you actually can't plug it in. It's entirely wireless. So you can actually program it over BLE.
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: The standard Arduino delay busy-waits at full current, so a battery-powered compatible board substitutes a sleep call that the programmer must use in place of the familiar delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: you find very quickly that you have to use, you know, bean.sleep instead of wait in your sketches
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: An ATmega running continuously draws a few milliamps, which rules out coin-cell operation unless the whole system is designed around sleeping the processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: running your, you know, at mega going a few milliamps is just terrible
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: A lower-power microcontroller was rejected for a battery-powered compatible board because keeping the ATmega meant existing Arduino code ran unchanged; source compatibility was valued above the power saving.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason we chose to stick with the AppMega and kind of standard Arduino experience is just so that people who've already written code for these Arduino platforms can just use the Bean, you know, without having to change anything
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: A vendor demonstrating a digital-interface part needs a host to talk to it, and standardising on one common platform avoids maintaining a separate demonstration board for every chip in the catalogue.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to standardize on some platform. Otherwise you have a different demo board for everything.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: Linear Technology's Linduino line is an Arduino-compatible demonstration board carrying sketches for the company's parts, priced around seventy-five dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: They've got one here for 75 bucks. You can buy the Arduino compatible demo board for this chip.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: Arduino shields are identified manually, the user selecting the matching library for whatever is plugged on, whereas the Raspberry Pi HAT scheme puts an EEPROM on the add-on so the host can identify it and configure the multiplexed pins itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just you know what board you've plugged on there, so you just choose the library for it and bam.
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: The Teensy offered USB human-interface-device capability with an Arduino-style development environment before the Arduino Leonardo did, letting a project emulate a keyboard or mouse directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: this was all inspired by the Teensy USB, which before the Arduino Leonardo had like its USB human input device set up on it
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Arduino was founded by five people who signed a contract assigning the trademark rights to the company itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they formed the company, Arduino, the five of them, they all signed a contract that said the company will own the rights to the trademark
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: One founder separately registered the Arduino trademark in Italy through his own company, so that entity held the Italian mark, which produced the split between arduino.cc and arduino.org and litigation between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: he went and trademarked Arduino in Italy
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: The trademark dispute was long-running rather than sudden: the other founders learned of the separate registration about a year after the company was formed and spent four or five years attempting to resolve it, with royalty payments having stopped twelve months before the matter became public.
claims.quote_verbatim: they found out like a year after they formed the company, they found out this guy went and trademarked the word Arduino on his own without telling the other founders
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: An open hardware project cannot be carried on donated effort the way a software project can, because physical boards must be manufactured and bought, which requires capital.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to purchase boards, you need actual capital
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: The dispute ended with the buy-out of Federico Musto, who controlled Arduino AG and with it the trademark, leaving Massimo Banzi's side owning the company and the mark outright.
claims.quote_verbatim: Federico Musto has been bought out. So now, Hasimo Banzi owns 100% of Arduino AG
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Where a shield communicates with its host over a plain serial link, the same board can be driven by anything else with a serial port, a single-board computer or a PC included, and the supplied Arduino library is only a convenience wrapper over documented low-level commands.
claims.quote_verbatim: the basic way the Arduino talks to the shield is actually via an RS 232 interface
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland of Audeme

claims.claim_text: The bottom of the Cortex-M0 range and the top of the ATmega range do not overlap: the smallest 32-bit ARM already offers more than the largest 8-bit part, so the migration is not a trade of one capability for another.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you look at a cortex m0 the very bottom of the cortex m0s the very top of the at mega chips they don't overlap i mean you get a lot more in the cortex m0
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: The concrete reasons for leaving the 8-bit Arduino-class part are clock speed, flash size, peripheral set and the integrated USB and LCD controllers; driving a 2.8-inch TFT over SPI from a 16 MHz part is slow enough to force a move to a parallel interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: just the speed and the flash size and the peripherals and the usb and the lcd peripherals is the main reason for sort of getting away from
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: An exact clone shares the original's software ecosystem, so work done on it feeds back to the same body of code; a merely similar board with its own drivers forms a separate, incompatible ecosystem.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino will be an exact clone. So anything you do there helps the Arduino community.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: Microchip's PIC became the hobbyist default because it was first with low-cost programming tools, including do-it-yourself serial-port programmers, at a time when other microcontroller vendors sold multi-thousand-dollar development systems.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were the first to come out with like low-cost tools that your regular Joe blogs could, you know, do
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Arduino's step beyond the low-cost programming tools that preceded it was ease of use rather than price alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino came along and said let's not only make it cheap, let's make it intuitive and easy
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Digilent moved its boards from AVR to Microchip's PIC32 early on for cost and performance reasons independent of Arduino compatibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: But then we moved over to microchip in the PIC32 line pretty early on. Nothing to do with Arduino. We just thought it was a better-costed, more performant processor.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: An undocumented serial LED protocol can be recovered by capturing the controller's data line with a logic analyser and then replaying the decoded stream from a microcontroller, which is how proprietary addressable light strings are driven without documentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I borrowed that from a friend and then cut it and figured out the data stream and then learned that I could use an Arduino to, to communicate this
claims.speaker: Samy Kamkar

claims.claim_text: For freelance client work the argument for the platform is handover: the toolchain is free, the client can find many people able to modify the result, and the consultant need not remain involved in future changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was a free tool chain you could get the most professional cc++ embedded programmer in the world or you could get um somebody who'd come through a design route and it gave my clients the ownership
claims.speaker: Stefan Dzisiewski-Smith

claims.claim_text: Choosing parts that already have established module and library support buys both supply availability and a choice of existing libraries for whoever maintains the design later.
claims.quote_verbatim: then we know that there's a reasonable established market you know that the availability of those parts is going to be reasonable and that there will be libraries that people will be able to access to take control of it themselves
claims.speaker: Stefan Dzisiewski-Smith

claims.claim_text: The Teensy's distinguishing value is a software layer over a much faster part, including an audio library in which audio connections are composed graphically, while the board can still be programmed as an Arduino or written in plain C.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a full-blown audio library where you can drag and drop audio connections on there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: In beginner workshops the first hour is routinely consumed by installing the development software, configuring it and connecting the board, overhead that a board presenting itself as a filesystem or a live interpreter removes.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first hour was just explaining to people how to install the software and how to get it set up and how to connect the boards
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: MicroPython follows desktop Python in letting time-critical or register-level work be written as C functions and called from Python as though they were native Python functions, so an interpreted program can still reach the hardware directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it does allow you to mix C and Python code
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: The SAMD NeoPixel driver was ported by taking the existing Arduino NeoPixel routine, which contains GCC inline assembly for the bit timing, wrapping it in the signature MicroPython expects and disabling interrupts around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we literally just took the Arduino NeoPixel code for the SamD processor, which was, uh, actually, uh, there is a little bit of assembly in that one
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: The Arduino toolchain is GCC driven from a graphical front end; enabling verbose output in the IDE exposes the compiler and upload commands actually being run.
claims.quote_verbatim: People don't realize that they're using GCC because it's all handled by the nice little GUI and everything else.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Boards that run MicroPython, the Atmel SAMD and ESP parts among them, also run Arduino, so the interpreter firmware can be erased and the board reused under the Arduino IDE if Python does not suit.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the boards that support MicroPython, at least the Atmel, SamD, and the ESP, they also support Arduino
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: The Arduino environment gained a compiler back end for the ESP8266, so the module can be programmed from the same IDE; before that the options were C or Lua.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino environment supports now has a compiler for the 8266 apparently
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The Arduino language is a thin surface over C++; the simplicity holds only until the user needs something the surface does not expose, at which point they are working in the underlying C++.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you get under the surface, you're in C++, which is pretty complicated
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: A shield supplied with unsoldered headers will not work when merely seated on the board: the pins must be soldered to the shield, a failure common enough to show up as returned kits.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to solder the headers to the shield, right?
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: The Arduino has no interpreter resident on the board, a common misconception: sketches are compiled on the host to native code and the machine code is what runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't have an interpreter on board. People think it does. But it doesn't. It just. It's just a C compiler.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: A protocol bit-banged from a general-purpose board may succeed only one attempt in ten, which is acceptable for a one-off investigation but not for a shipping product, where reliability, repeatability and manufacturability narrow the usable set of techniques sharply.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can bit bang a protocol with an Arduino and have it work, you know, one in ten times, and that's a valid attack
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: A dependable way to control a proprietary radio device is to gut one of its factory remote controls and wire across the back of its buttons, driving them from a shield's outputs; the weakness is the labour and the fragility of the jumper wiring.
claims.quote_verbatim: rip out one of the factory remote controls and just wire across the back of the buttons and trigger it and send the signal
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: Consumer remote controls cluster in the unlicensed bands, mainly 433 MHz and 315 MHz with the choice country-dependent, so a receiver shield presenting the raw demodulated waveform is enough to reverse-engineer garage door openers, remote power boards and wireless weather stations.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's 433 megahertz and a couple of others, 315 megahertz. It's country dependent.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: The platform started on the AVR, but because the compiler sits hidden behind the graphical front end the underlying architecture became irrelevant to the user, and PIC- and ARM-based boards followed.
claims.quote_verbatim: integrate the compiler hidden behind the GUI interface. It doesn't matter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One autopilot project dropped AVR support around 2008 and moved to the STM32 because fitting the code onto the 8-bit part required disabling most of the functionality.
claims.quote_verbatim: We dropped AVR support because you barely could run any – like you had to really disable most of the functionality to be able to put it on that platform.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Autopilot hardware carried a CAN bus for communication between aircraft subsystems before standards for UAV CAN communication existed.
claims.quote_verbatim: having a CAN bus on the aircraft or on the autopilot because they want a secure communication between the subsystems
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: A common commercial route is to prove the product fully functional on an Arduino and then hand it to an embedded engineer who reimplements it on a production microcontroller such as a PIC.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have fully – got the product fully functional with an Arduino. Sure. And then I send it off to an embedded guy who converts the whole thing over to a pick chip.
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: The concentrated value of the platform is its central tool rather than its hardware, and that is also the concentrated risk: the hardware varied across the ecosystem, but the loss of the single development environment would have affected every dependent product.
claims.quote_verbatim: the centralized tool of Arduino is the real value there, right? The hardware was varied throughout the ecosystem and ultimately didn't matter as much
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Arduino code is compiled ahead of time: it is C and C++ underneath, transformed into valid C before compilation, so the desktop machine does the optimising and what reaches the board is instructions the processor executes directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino is C, C plus plus under the hood. They do some funny tricks to make it proper C before they actually compile it.
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: For speed and power the compiled Arduino path outperforms CircuitPython, with MicroPython between them; the attached advice is not to optimise before establishing that the interpreted option is actually too slow.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino is better about power and speed and micro Python is better as well
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: A retro computer kit with only a mask ROM and static RAM can be loaded without reprogramming the ROM by bit-banging a serial stream from a microcontroller into its joystick port, using the loader already in the ROM; the program is lost at power-down because there is no non-volatile storage.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can hook the joystick port up to an Arduino, which then bit bangs in serial stuff and they've got an old school loader built into the ROM.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In practice the name denotes a compatibility layer rather than a specific chip: it is a common target meaning straightforward microcontroller work regardless of the silicon underneath.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino name is, it's a brand, it's a movement, it's, you know, it's a compatible, a compatibility layer
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: There is no Arduino microcontroller: the Arduino is a board standard plus the development environment on top of it, and the part underneath the classic boards is an Atmel AVR.
claims.quote_verbatim: We should disambiguate as well because there's not an Arduino microcontroller. The Arduino is the standard and the IDE on top of it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The platform's defining property is that it abstracts the microcontroller away from the user, which is at once the source of its accessibility and of what its users never learn about the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: the problem with the Arduino is that it's higher level and it abstracts out the microcontroller
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The PIC 16F84 replaced the EEPROM-programmed 16C84 with flash while keeping in-circuit reprogramming, and a programmer that hooked to a PC serial port is what first put low-cost microcontroller development within reach of individuals.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then they came out with the 16F84, which was the Flash version, but it did the same thing, but it used Flash instead of E-squared PROM.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Arduino applies two abstractions at once: the user need not know which processor is fitted, and input and output are performed by calling a written routine such as digitalWrite instead of writing the port register directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than use the direct instruction to write to the IO port, you call up an already written routine, which is just a C routine, which writes to the port for you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because every sketch reaches the hardware through those routines, the same source runs on an Atmel, a PIC, an ARM, an MSP430 or an Espressif part without change; the portability is a property of the library layer, not of the language.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it doesn't matter whether it's an Atmel, a PIC, an ARM, or an MSP430 or expressive or whatever it is. It doesn't matter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: By the late 2010s an Arduino-compatible board could be bought for around two dollars delivered, which is the price context for any argument about designing one out of a product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can buy an Arduino for, what, a couple of bucks on eBay delivered? Two bucks.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A twelve-degree-of-freedom quadruped can be run from 8-bit Arduinos computing inverse kinematics for every joint at once, commanded through a six-axis controller built from two three-axis joysticks covering translation, roll, pitch and yaw.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it calculates the inverse kinematics for all of the joints all at once.
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: Moving that control from 16 MHz 8-bit boards to 180 MHz 32-bit Teensy boards is better than a tenfold increase in clock rate for the same code base.
claims.quote_verbatim: which are due to get upgraded to teensies, which are 32-bit and 180 megahertz instead of 16 megahertz
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: A requirement for six serial ports forced a three-board architecture, one master Arduino feeding two slaves, which a single CAN bus controller replaces once the motor drivers support CAN.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got one master Arduino. And then that sends serial to two slave Arduinos. And that's because I need six serial ports.
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: The Intel Galileo carried an x86 core but emulated the Arduino input and output through an I2C expander, which made pin operations very slow despite the more powerful processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: it used like I squared C to emulate the IO of an Arduino. It was so slow.
claims.speaker: Ben Heck

claims.claim_text: A modular board plugged together through a known header is right for prototyping and usually wrong for production: connectors add cost, the form factor is not optimised for the enclosure and power consumption is not tuned, unless the product is a high-margin niche item where a module's cost does not matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: Adding, adding connectors adds, adds cost.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The claim that the platform does not scale needs qualification: because the design is open, it can be stripped back to the bare microcontroller and reproduced cheaply, so the scaling limit lies in the system architecture rather than in the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not that you can't take an Arduino design and then repackage it cheaply because you can do that because it's open source.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: When a prototype assembled from off-the-shelf boards is to be built two hundred times, consolidating everything onto one printed circuit board and resolving the connectors is easier than replicating a cabled stack of dev boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be much easier to stick everything on one PCB and sort out all the connectors and everything
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Stackable pin headers in the Arduino style and castellated board edges are the two module interfaces usable across the widest range of applications, whereas schemes needing press-fit studs and separate mounting hardware add parts and assembly steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: the stackable pin header, you know, like your Arduino style or the, or the castellation side of the board style, you know? So yeah, they're just more usable in more applications.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Connecting a servo motor directly to a microcontroller input-output pin is a characteristic intermediate-level failure, and knowing to insert a driver stage is exactly the gap between making an LED blink and building a working machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time I plugged a servo directly into the IO pin
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The usual progression is from the Arduino board to designing one's own microcontroller board with surface-mount parts, which is the step at which producibility and layout practice first matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: going from Arduino to making something more producible or something that looks more professional
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: The SAMD21's appeal for education-oriented boards is that it is an automotive-grade part with an on-board DAC, ruggedised peripherals and generous memory, which matters when users will connect things wrongly; it is not a cheap part.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think that's why Lamore favors them is because there's a DAC on board. And, you know, the peripherals are very ruggedized
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A library that includes Arduino.h with the wrong letter case compiles on a case-insensitive Windows filesystem and fails on Linux, a portability failure that presents as a bug in whatever tool first exposes it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the author of the library included Arduino dot H with without a capital A. So if you compile it on a Windows computer, it works. But when you compile it on Linux, it breaks.
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: A browser-based Arduino simulator compiles the sketch server-side with the Arduino command-line interface to exactly the hex file a local build would produce, then executes that hex in an AVR instruction-set simulator in the browser.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses the Arduino CLI on that server to compile that source code into a hex file. And it's the same hex file that you would get if you compile the code on your machine
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: analogWrite does not generate a waveform in software: it configures the hardware timer registers, and on the Uno which of timers 0, 1 and 2 is used depends on which pin was named.
claims.quote_verbatim: that function will write to the timer registers. So depending on the pin, that would be timer 0, 1, or 2 on Arduino Uno.
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: Perceived brightness under pulse-width modulation is not linear in duty cycle: rendering it faithfully means taking a moving average of on-time per frame and applying a gamma correction, so a thirty per cent duty cycle appears at roughly seventy per cent.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if it sees like it was on 30% of the time, it will set the opacity of the layer that represents the light of the LED, not exactly to 30%, because it also applies gamma calculation.
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: The compile-and-upload cycle repeats on every change, whereas an interpreted runtime is loaded once and then updated interactively, which removes a recompilation from every iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: When you develop locally with Arduino, you have to compile and upload the code each time, right? But when you use MicroPython, you just load MicroPython once into the board
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: The Arduino Mega outline persists in 3D printers, where aftermarket controller boards carrying stepper drivers plug on top of it as shields; that installed base is what makes a faster board in the same outline a useful upgrade.
claims.quote_verbatim: you see things like the Mega, which is the form factor, being used in things like 3D printers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A very fast part behind a simple interface lets a super-loop program be sped up by hardware instead of by optimisation, which is convenient but spends silicon on work that code changes could have absorbed.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's so much horsepower being put at like tasks that could be optimized in code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The cost floor for a USB-attached microcontroller gadget was an STM32F042 at seventy to eighty cents or an ATmega32U4 at about a dollar forty; a ten-cent part with the same capability removes the cost argument against embedding one anywhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: Normally you need something which is a minimum of an STM 32 F Oh four two at 70 cents, or I guess that's what 80 cents now.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: USB can be bit-banged in software on a fast enough part: on a 160 MHz ESP8266 a low-speed device was implemented by reading or writing one bus bit every 53.333 cycles and running the protocol in firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: every 53.333 cycles, don't worry about how that works. You go either write or read a bit on the USB bus
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The threshold that makes a cheap part usable in the Arduino sense is being able to flash it over USB without a separate programmer.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I can turn this into an Arduino where I can flash the part over USB, so I don't need a programmer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The Arduino ecosystem rests on a backend index describing available boards and pullable libraries, and most sensor vendors now ship Arduino drivers, so straightforward example code exists for a part before any other framework has support for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of vendors finally jumped on board and like, oh, well we have Arduino drivers too, right? We make sensors, we have Arduino libraries
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: ESP modules cost a dollar or two alone and finished development boards using them sell in three-packs for eight to twelve dollars, which is the price level at which designing a home-automation node from scratch stops paying.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ESP modules themselves are, you know, a dollar or two for just the module
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Arduino sells about two million boards a year and still takes roughly eighty per cent of its income from hardware, against some fifty million dollars of venture capital raised.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino sell about 2 million boards a year. Most of their income comes from hardware. About 80% of their income comes from hardware sales still.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: mbed OS was sustained by ARM paying its own engineers to write vendor support across parts from different silicon vendors; when that funding stopped the ecosystem reached end of life, and Zephyr activity rose over the same period.
claims.quote_verbatim: ARM was the one that was driving all that stuff where they would pay their engineers to do a compatibility for an NRF 52 versus a STM 32
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A sketch-level API still needs an operating-system layer beneath it to carry networking stacks, since vendors do not abstract at that level themselves; that requirement is why the platform moved from mbed to Zephyr.
claims.quote_verbatim: You need some kind of like OS layer thing to, to hand, hand the data down over the various networking layers.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Zephyr's linkable loadable extensions allow code to be loaded at runtime onto an already-running system, which fits the sketch model exactly: the plumbing stays resident and the user's sketch is hot-swapped in on top of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: at runtime, you can actually load in these linkable, loadable extensions, right? You could have kind of dynamic memory slot in there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The Uno Q sells for about forty-four dollars, in line with what Raspberry Pi boards cost after successive price rises driven by memory cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: $44 for like a monster machine, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A bootloader can be the commercial asset of an otherwise open board: PJRC keeps the Teensy bootloader closed because giving it away would remove the reason to buy the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't do that if you just give away the bootloader because who's going to buy it from you?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The Teensy is a compatibility layer that keeps the Arduino programming model while substituting a far faster part, an i.MX RT in place of an ATmega328P, so an existing super-loop program can simply be run faster without restructuring.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically an IMX RT part on there is, you know, it's something like 4600x faster
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The platform descends from a 2003 prototyping board and from Wiring, a student thesis project, which were rebuilt into a new platform by Massimo Banzi, Tom Igoe, David Cuartielles and David Mellis.
claims.quote_verbatim: he built this project called Wiring and then me, Tom, David, and one of my students, David Mellis
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The development environment was made by taking Processing, a language and environment built for designers and artists to program desktop computers, removing Java and substituting C++.
claims.quote_verbatim: we made this development environment which is basically was their development environment with Java removed and plugged with C++
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing was local from the start: Ivrea, the site of Olivetti's electronics industry for decades, still had board fabrication and assembly within a fifteen-minute drive, and Arduino still manufactures a large share of its production there.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had to drive 15 minutes to get to the PCB factory.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The open licence was applied to the hardware deliberately, before the term open-source hardware existed, so that others could build on the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: It needed to be open source hardware. We didn't know that thing existed, but we wanted to apply like a license to hardware
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: Examples were written into the environment itself rather than left to be found, two weeks being spent on them before release, on the reasoning that a beginner opens an example, runs it, and then changes one number to see what happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: we spent basically two weeks in the summer just writing a ton of examples because the idea is I want the example baked into the idea. I don't want people to have to find them.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The IDE was deliberately held to seven buttons for twenty years, a product decision taken by interaction designers rather than a technical constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why the IDE for 20 years has got seven buttons.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The name comes from a bar in Ivrea named after a local king, and the term shield followed from the observation that a board stacking on top of an Arduino is a king's shield.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we are making a circuit that stacks on top of the Arduino, that's the shield of a king
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The stacking format worked because a third party need only make a plain printed circuit board and place it on top, and the irregular outline had the side effect of making the board recognisable and helping the user orient it.
claims.quote_verbatim: because you just make a PCB and you stick it on top and it works
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The first motor shield was derived from a shield originally built for Wiring, and further shields were driven by the interface needs of paid interactive-installation work for exhibitions.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first motor shield was actually a derivation of the shield that we built for wiring
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The structural problem for an open hardware company is that value accrues to the silicon vendor and to cloners rather than to the platform: Atmel and later Microchip kept selling large volumes of the ATmega328 while the boards themselves were copied.
claims.quote_verbatim: the people who make the chips, they make all the money in the end, you know, or because your product gets cloned a million times
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The design principle is layered encapsulation: blinking an LED takes about seven lines at the top layer, and a user needing more control strips a layer to reach a more granular API, and can descend further to plain C on the microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: in Arduino, you can strip a layer, and now you are operating one layer down, and you have much more granular API
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The top layer's encapsulation is explicitly acknowledged as quick and productive but not optimal; the cost of the abstraction is accepted in exchange for a beginner reaching a working result.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a very high level of encapsulation. Obviously, that is very quick, very productive, but maybe not optimal.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The Uno Q is a compact Linux machine wrapped in tooling built on containers and micro-containers, so that the user works entirely through the tools and never touches Linux directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is a super compact Linux machine, but they developed all this tooling around it that you can build incredible things, and you don't touch Linux at all.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: Porting Grbl from an 8-bit Arduino target to a 32-bit part is close to drag-and-drop for the motion planner because both are C; the work lies in bringing up the peripherals first, three timers, a PWM channel and the interrupt and pulse handling, after which the rest plugs in.
claims.quote_verbatim: I worked from the outside in, I needed all these peripherals and I said, okay, I need, you know, three timers. I needed a PWM
claims.speaker: Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: A controller part without integrated radios forces extra modules and interconnect onto the board; the ESP32 displaced one such design by combining a cheap, small package with the radios already on chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: the PSoC five didn't have Bluetooth. It didn't have wifi. So I'm adding more modules. It's getting more complicated.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Once a module and a library exist, a formerly specialist task collapses to a few lines: receiving an SMS on a microcontroller and displaying it on an LCD takes about ten lines of code.
claims.quote_verbatim: anyone can just send an SMS to their Arduino and it pops up on an LCD with ten lines of code
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Glass and Gongkai GSM - Unzymotic Ursidae Upbuilding

claims.claim_text: A shield can bridge into a proprietary ecosystem: one exposing the Lego Mindstorms NXT connector let the light sensors, touch sensors, motors and motor encoders be read and driven from Arduino code, pairing Lego's mechanical prototyping speed with the electronics side.
claims.quote_verbatim: we made a shield for the Arduino that lets you hook up everything that's in a Lego Mindstorms NXT box into an Arduino
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A product can ship in its earliest form without a designed circuit board at all: the first units of one commercial robot used an Arduino, a shield, a mini breadboard and six jumper wires in place of a board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the circuit board was literally an Arduino and then a shield and then a, uh, one of those little mini breadboards and like six wires to connect up
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: The platform's software was formally pre-release until version 1.0, and the 1.0 API change broke a large part of the existing third-party library base, which then had to be rewritten.
claims.quote_verbatim: all these hundreds of thousands of libraries people have written all out there, right? Yeah. But a good lot of them now are useless. They have to be rewritten.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because the part underneath is an ordinary AVR, a design built on the Arduino layer retains the fallback of programming the same silicon directly in C.
claims.quote_verbatim: because it's just an AVR. If I don't like it, I can always, you know, I didn't like it. Or somebody doesn't like it, they can always go back and program directly in C
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Breaking an API in a beginner-facing platform carries an outsized cost: the beginner downloads existing example code, the compile fails, and the failure surfaces as cryptic C++ error messages that give no route forward.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're a beginner, you download it, compile, fail, doesn't work. Gives you all these cryptic C++ error messages.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The dominant attraction of the platform is the volume of existing example code, which makes backwards compatibility of that code the property that matters most in any release.
claims.quote_verbatim: if there's one big attraction to Arduino, it is the fact that there's so many people using it and so much existing example code out there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The minimum Arduino-compatible hardware is close to the microcontroller alone, which is why an Uno can be shrunk to roughly the footprint of the chip it carries.
claims.quote_verbatim: we took an Arduino Uno, shrunk it down to the size of a chip.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: The Arduino's power design is a single wall supply linearly regulated to five volts, whereas an FPGA-class design needs separate rails around one volt for the core, 1.8 V for high-speed transceivers, 2.5 V, and 3.3 V for input and output, with seven or eight rails not unusual.
claims.quote_verbatim: They need a 1.8 volt for the high speed transceivers. They need a 2.5 for something else. And they need a 3.3 for the IO.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A bare-board product avoids the largest fixed costs of a consumer product, enclosure tooling, plastics and finishing, because the panelised board snapped apart is the finished item; that is a substantial part of why development boards are cheap.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're really cheap because you don't have to worry about an external case or anything like that. You just manufacture the board and snap them off the panel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Volume in the hobby channel is small in silicon terms, on the order of a hundred thousand boards across about five years, so presence on a development board is a poor proxy for a part's production volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Arduino has only made a hundred thousand over the last, you know, five years. That's not many. That's a drop in the bucket for at mail.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Freescale, Hackerspaces, Printable Electronics - Publish Popular Parts Please!

claims.claim_text: A bare board with parts on it offers no differentiation against a copy beyond branding, whereas a product with an enclosure differs in mechanical CAD, plastics, switch feel and layout, because a cloner would have to redo all of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: what is the difference between a genuine Arduino and one of the clone ones or whatever you want to call them? Right. Nothing. Cause it's a bare board with parts on it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: An undocumented sensor initialisation can be recovered by capturing its I2C traffic, decoding it against a database-driven register map so each read and write is labelled with register and bit fields, then writing a sketch that reproduces the identical transaction sequence.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was just a matter of building an Arduino script that imitated the exact same set of, of, uh, transactions
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master
